clue.text: Put one's foot down when presented with energy charge

parts.note: to bring a foot down hard is to stamp, in the past tense here
E is the physics symbol for energy

explanation.surface: Someone gets firm and refuses to budge on a bill that includes their energy costs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put one's foot down' reads as taking a stand, but here it is a literal stamp; 'charge' is a fee in the surface and a headlong rush in the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A charge is a sudden rush forward, and a stampede is a panicked headlong rush of a herd or crowd.

clue.text: Place is upside-down by half-term

indicators.note: in a down entry, turning upside-down means the word is read from the bottom up

parts.note: taken as written before being turned over

indicators.note: half of a four-letter word keeps only two of its letters, here the opening pair

parts.note: the front half of this word

explanation.surface: Something has been turned upside-down by the time half-term arrives, as any parent knows.
explanation.walkthrough: Half-term is a short British school holiday; the hyphenated word splits into a selection signal and the word it acts on.
explanation.definitionFit: A site is a location or plot where something stands or happens, a straightforward synonym for a place.

clue.text: All eager for a try before start of game

parts.note: A as written, plus GO, a try or attempt

indicators.note: the start of a word is its opening letter alone

parts.note: the opening letter of game

explanation.surface: Everyone is keen to have a go before the game kicks off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'All agog' is a set phrase, so the definition takes in 'All'.
explanation.definitionFit: Agog describes being excitedly expectant, keenly waiting to see or hear something, so 'all eager' matches the idiom.

clue.text: Ghastly look of some municipal lorries

indicators.note: some of the following words means only a stretch of their letters is wanted

parts.note: the letters run from the end of the first word into the start of the second

explanation.surface: Council bin lorries have a grim appearance.
explanation.definitionFit: Pallor is an unhealthy paleness of the face, the ghastly look of someone ill or frightened.

clue.text: No one should meddle with this internationally sensitive case

definitions.text: No one should meddle with this internationally sensitive case

parts.words: No one should meddle with this internationally sensitive case
parts.note: surface reading: a delicate diplomatic dispute between nations that outsiders should leave alone
setter's reading: a case is a container, here a sealed pouch for embassy documents that customs may not open

explanation.walkthrough: 'Case' suggests an affair or incident; it is in fact luggage protected by international law.
explanation.definitionFit: Such a pouch carries official embassy correspondence and is immune from search under the Vienna Convention, so nobody may tamper with it.

clue.text: Made up for being poorly prepared

parts.note: feeling off is feeling unwell
ready, as in 'all set'

explanation.surface: Someone compensated for having turned up unready.
explanation.definitionFit: To offset is to counterbalance or compensate, so a loss that was offset was made up for.

clue.text: Delight when life model goes to town

indicators.note: to model is to shape or fashion, so the preceding word is moulded into a new order
one piece goes on to join the next, placing them side by side

parts.note: these four letters rearranged
a large town is a city

explanation.surface: An artist's model enjoys a day out in town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Life model' reads as an artist's sitter; the two words have separate jobs.
explanation.definitionFit: Felicity is intense happiness or bliss, a slightly formal word for great joy.

clue.text: Son confused as mice ate feline

indicators.note: confused letters are jumbled out of their proper order

parts.note: S is the standard abbreviation for son
nine letters jumbled

explanation.surface: A boy is baffled because some mice ate the cat.
explanation.walkthrough: The absurd scene of mice devouring a cat hides that the cat is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a pale, blue-eyed breed of domestic cat from Thailand, so it is a feline by example.

clue.text: Reaching across tabletop, partygoers spilt gin

indicators.note: spilt drink splashes everywhere, so its letters land in a mess
the top of a down word is its first letter

parts.note: the first letter of table
people at a rave are ravers
three letters rearranged

explanation.surface: At a party, someone stretches over the table and revellers knock over the gin.
explanation.definitionFit: Traversing means crossing or travelling over something, so it means going or reaching across.

clue.text: Goodbye said to old rogue on Tube returning

indicators.note: returning means going back, so the word for Tube runs backwards
rogue as an adjective means wayward, so the two short words before it go astray

parts.note: five letters rearranged
a pipe is a tube

explanation.surface: A farewell is spoken to an elderly scoundrel travelling home on the London Underground.
explanation.walkthrough: TOODL then PIPE reversed as EPIP; the Tube is London's Underground, but here it is just a pipe.
explanation.definitionFit: Toodle-pip is jaunty, old-fashioned British slang for farewell, like cheerio.

clue.text: One demands the best — often priciest — variety

indicators.note: a variety is a different version, so the letters before it appear in a different arrangement

parts.note: thirteen letters rearranged

explanation.surface: A demanding shopper insists on the best, which often means the most expensive kind.
explanation.definitionFit: A perfectionist is someone who refuses anything short of flawless, so they insist on top quality.

clue.text: Girl, I gathered, finds something creepy in the forest

indicators.note: to gather something in is to take it inside, so the girl's name holds the letter

parts.note: a girl's name
taken as written

explanation.surface: A girl, as I understood it, stumbles on something spooky in the woods.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Creepy' suggests scary, but it means creeping, as a climbing plant does.
explanation.definitionFit: A liana is a woody climbing vine of tropical forests, which creeps up tree trunks.

clue.text: Bias against programme in black and white, for instance

indicators.note: against means up against, set alongside, so the two parts sit next to each other

parts.note: to colour a judgement is to bias it
a plan or programme of action

explanation.surface: Someone objects to a TV programme being shown in black and white.
explanation.definitionFit: A pairing of black and white is an example of a chosen combination of hues for a design.

clue.text: Christian symbol remains a reminder of mortality

parts.note: the emblem of Christianity
a skeleton's remains

explanation.surface: A religious emblem serves as a reminder that we all die.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Remains' looks like a verb, as in 'stays', but it is a noun.
explanation.definitionFit: Crossed bones beneath a skull are a traditional memento mori, an emblem of death on graves and pirate flags.

clue.text: It keeps one going when all at sea

definitions.text: It keeps one going when all at sea

parts.words: It keeps one going when all at sea
parts.note: surface reading: something that keeps a person's spirits up when they are confused or bewildered
setter's reading: literally on the ocean, where a compartment of a ship houses what drives it

explanation.walkthrough: 'All at sea' is the idiom for being lost and confused; read literally it is a ship on the water.
explanation.definitionFit: This compartment holds a vessel's propulsion machinery, which literally keeps the boat moving on the ocean.

clue.text: Run-in with leading girl band

parts.note: R is the cricket abbreviation for run
taken as written

indicators.note: the leading letter of a word is the one at its front

parts.note: the first letter of girl

explanation.surface: There is a quarrel involving the frontwoman of a girl band.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Run-in' looks like one word meaning a row; the hyphen hides two separate pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: A ring is a circular band, such as the one worn on a finger.

clue.text: Hardy heroine receives letters from all ten, without a single gift!

indicators.note: the letters from the phrase are used in a new order rather than as written
one who receives takes something in, so the heroine's name holds the other letters

parts.note: Tess of the d'Urbervilles, Thomas Hardy's heroine
six letters rearranged

explanation.surface: Tess gets letters from all ten admirers, yet not one present.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gift' reads as a present; it means a natural ability.
explanation.definitionFit: Talentless describes someone with no natural aptitude, since a gift can mean an innate ability or flair.

clue.text: Scrutiny of very particular year sister joined

indicators.note: the pieces are joined end to end, one after another

parts.note: informal for obsessively fussy
Y is the abbreviation for year
short for sister

explanation.surface: A sister who arrived in a particular year comes under close examination.
explanation.definitionFit: Analysis is the detailed examination of something's parts, a close and careful study.

clue.text: Insect damage is found on backstreet, reveal researchers

indicators.note: found on means placed next to, so the pieces follow in turn

parts.note: six letters rearranged

indicators.note: back means the abbreviation for street is read backwards
damaged letters are knocked out of shape and rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
ST is the abbreviation for street, the word after the reversal signal

explanation.surface: Damage caused by insects in a back street is uncovered by experts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Backstreet' reads as one word; it splits into a reversal signal and the street, giving TS.
explanation.definitionFit: Scientists carry out systematic investigation and experiment, so they are people who do research.

clue.text: Irritation of one in short sleepover

indicators.note: turned over means flipped round, so the word is read backwards
in places the single letter inside the other word

parts.note: a nap is a short sleep; the last four letters are the reversal signal
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Someone is annoyed by a guest at a brief overnight stay.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sleepover' reads as one word, but 'over' is split off to reverse NAP to PAN, and I goes in.
explanation.definitionFit: A pain, as in 'a pain in the neck', is a nuisance or something annoying.

clue.text: Clerical assistant gets right up to the margin

indicators.note: in a down entry, going up to means placed right below, so the pieces sit end to end

parts.note: a verge is an edge or border
R is the abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: An office helper fills the page right to the edge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Clerical' suggests office work; it means of the clergy.
explanation.definitionFit: A verger is a church official who looks after the building and assists the priest during services.

clue.text: Frowning, one of Fab Four heard brother was in debt

indicators.note: heard means the word is taken by its sound, not its spelling

parts.note: the Fab Four were the Beatles; the insect sounds the same
BR is the abbreviation for brother
to be in debt is to owe money

explanation.surface: A member of the Beatles scowls on learning his brother owed money.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone with heavy, overhanging brows looks sullen, so the adjective describes a scowling or glowering face.

clue.text: Shape of both clutch and headlight

parts.note: a clutch is a set of eggs, and ova are eggs

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter

parts.note: the first letter of light, after the selection signal

explanation.surface: A car part puzzle: what outline do the clutch pedal and headlamp share?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Clutch' and 'headlight' suggest car parts; a clutch is a batch of eggs, and the head of light is its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: An oval is an elongated rounded outline, the shape of an egg, which ties both parts together.

clue.text: Hard work is pointless — but it's where setters begin

indicators.note: without a point means losing a compass direction letter

parts.note: a grind is tedious, hard work

explanation.surface: Hard toil seems futile, yet it is where crossword compilers start.
explanation.walkthrough: A point is a compass point, so N (north) comes out of GRIND.
explanation.definitionFit: A setter, the compiler of a crossword, starts by filling the pattern of black and white squares.

clue.text: New unopened volumes found in hiding places

indicators.note: something unopened has lost its opening, so the word drops its first letter

parts.note: N is the abbreviation for new
volumes are books

explanation.surface: Brand-new books still in their wrapping are discovered tucked away.
explanation.definitionFit: Nooks are small sheltered corners or recesses, the sort of spots where things are concealed.

clue.text: On the way out, concluded careful inspection

parts.note: something going is leaving or departing
finished or ended

explanation.surface: As someone was leaving, they finished a thorough check.
explanation.definitionFit: A going-over is a thorough examination or check, as when a mechanic examines a car closely.

clue.text: Pacific islands import south Indian food

indicators.note: to import is to bring something inside, so the islands take in the letter

parts.note: Samoa is an island group in the South Pacific
S is the abbreviation for south

explanation.surface: Islands in the Pacific bring in food from southern India.
explanation.walkthrough: 'South Indian' looks like one description of the food; 'south' belongs to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A samosa is a fried triangular pastry with a spiced filling, a popular snack from the subcontinent.

clue.text: Taken aback from the outset, having been in charge

parts.note: the outset is the beginning
to be in charge is to lead, past tense

explanation.surface: Someone who had been in charge from the beginning is caught by surprise.
explanation.definitionFit: Startled means surprised and alarmed, which is the sense of the idiom about being shocked.
